params.prompt: Theo holds a Maryland license. An insurer now offers A M G a producer agreement. Three documents are in play, and they are not the same. The license is the state’s permission to act as a producer in Maryland. The producer agreement is the business contract setting commissions, duties and termination terms. The appointment is the insurer’s registration of Theo as its agent, recorded in the insurer’s producer register under Maryland law. A producer may hold a license and a contract and still lack an appointment. Only the appointment makes him the insurer’s agent for the acts the statute requires an appointment for.

Appointments attach to people and to entities. The insurer appoints A M G, the business entity, and it appoints each individual producer who will act for it; an agency appointment does not by itself make every employee an appointed agent of the insurer. Theo should confirm that his own name is in the insurer’s register, not only A M G’s. When a producer leaves one agency for another, the appointment through the old agency ends and a new appointment is needed. Appointment is also line-specific: an appointment for life business does not authorize health solicitation unless the insurer’s register covers it.

Maryland lets a licensed producer solicit an application for an insurer authorized for that line without first being appointed. The protection kicks in when the insurer accepts the application: within thirty days it must either reject the application or appoint the producer and enter the required information in its register. So Theo may bring a first health application to a carrier he has never worked with, but the carrier may not keep accepting his business without appointing him. Accepting an application for processing is not acceptance of the risk and does not mean coverage has begun.

Once it appoints Theo, the insurer enters the appointment in its producer register within thirty days and gives him written documentation of the appointment within thirty days. Theo keeps that documentation and a list of every insurer that has appointed him. With the written documentation in hand he may act within his authority even before the register entry is complete. Appointment records stay available while the appointment is active and for at least five years after it ends, and electronic records must be retrievable within ten working days of the Commissioner’s request. A screenshot no one can find later is not a record.

An insurer that terminates an appointment updates its register within thirty days after the effective date. If the termination is for a reason that could be grounds for discipline, the insurer must also notify the Commissioner, send Theo a copy within fifteen days after that notice, and Theo then has thirty days after receiving it to submit comments, with a copy to the insurer. Once his appointment ends he must cease soliciting for that insurer immediately; a pending commission does not extend his authority. Ending an appointment is the insurer’s decision and does not revoke his license; only the Commissioner can do that.

Theo’s license stays valid even if no insurer has appointed him. He may keep it active through renewal and continuing education and may solicit applications that an insurer must then accept and appoint or reject. What he may not do is hold himself out as an insurer’s agent, bind coverage or collect premium for an insurer that has not appointed him. For every appointment question, name the actor and the clock: the producer solicits; the insurer accepts, appoints within thirty days, documents within thirty days, keeps records five years, and on termination updates the register within thirty days and notifies the Commissioner when discipline grounds exist.

Section ten dash one twenty-six lists what can cost Theo his license. Making an intentional material misstatement on a license application. Obtaining or trying to obtain a license through fraud. Violating the Insurance Article or a Commissioner’s order. Misappropriating, converting or unlawfully withholding money belonging to an insurer, insured or applicant. Intentionally misrepresenting the terms of a policy. Forging an insurance document. Being convicted of a felony or a crime of moral turpitude. Demonstrating a lack of trustworthiness or competence. Failing to obey a lawful order or subpoena. Having a license disciplined in another state. Failing to report as required. Any of these supports action against the license.

After notice and an opportunity for a hearing, the Commissioner may refuse to issue or renew a license, place the licensee on probation with conditions, suspend the license for a period, or revoke it. Each has a different effect: a suspended producer may return when the period ends; a revoked producer must reapply and may be refused. Instead of or in addition to suspension or revocation, the Commissioner may impose a penalty of one hundred to five thousand dollars for each violation and may order restitution to anyone who suffered a financial loss. The Commissioner may also issue a cease-and-desist order requiring a person to stop a specific unlawful practice, with further penalties for ignoring it.

Due process shapes the procedure. Before most license sanctions, the Commissioner gives written notice of the proposed action and the grounds, and the licensee may demand a hearing. Under Section two dash two ten, a written hearing demand states the grounds for the request; the Commissioner must grant and hold the hearing within thirty consecutive days, unless the parties agree to postpone it, or refuse it, and a failure to act is treated as a refusal. At the hearing the producer may appear, present evidence and be represented. The Commissioner then issues a written order. Where the public faces immediate danger, the law permits summary action followed by a prompt hearing.

A producer who loses before the Commissioner is not finished. Under Section two dash two fifteen a petition for judicial review in the circuit court is generally due within thirty days after the order is served, or after a refusal to hold a hearing. The court reviews the record for legal error and substantial evidence; it does not retry the case. Filing the petition does not automatically stay the Commissioner’s order, so a revoked producer stays revoked unless the court grants a stay. Theo’s practical lesson: respond to every notice, keep records that show what actually happened, and never ignore a lawful order or request for records while a matter is pending.

Insurance fraud is knowingly presenting a false or misleading statement, claim or document to obtain a benefit, premium, commission or coverage. It includes padding a disability claim, backdating an application, pocketing a premium, or helping a client misstate health history. Maryland prosecutes insurance fraud criminally, with penalties that rise with the amount involved and can include prison, and the Commissioner can add administrative penalties and restitution. The Insurance Fraud Division, created under Section two dash four oh one within the Administration, investigates suspected fraud and refers cases for prosecution. Producers are frequent targets of fraud and frequent sources of the evidence that stops it.

Section twenty-seven dash eight oh two requires a person with good-faith cause to believe insurance fraud has occurred to report it in writing; an independent producer reports to the Fraud Division, and producers working for an insurer report through the insurer’s anti-fraud process. Good-faith reports are protected from civil liability; knowingly false accusations are not. When Theo suspects a client inflated a claim, he does not quietly withdraw and hope; he preserves the facts, follows the reporting process and cooperates with the Division. Concealing suspected fraud to protect a commission is itself a path to discipline under Section ten dash one twenty-six.
